raw_response.overlap_rationale: Study A (Switzer & Teodoro 2025) and Study B (Zhang, González Rivas, Grant & Warner 2022) are independent studies by unrelated author teams that collected primary residential water rate schedules four years apart (January–April 2019 in Study A vs. January 2015 in Study B) and analyze distinct outcomes, but share a nested subset of approximately 500 large US community water systems. Specifically, both studies draw deterministic top-size censuses of US community water systems from the US EPA Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS): Study A examines all 1,189 US utilities serving >= 40,000 residents (N = 1,183 in contiguous 48 states, serving 183.3 million people; ln(population) range 10.60 to 15.93), while Study B examines the 500 largest US community water systems across 48 states and DC (serving ~140 million people; ln(service population) range 11.36 [~85,800 residents] to 15.93). Consequently, nearly all 500 utilities in Study B are nested within Study A's 1,183-utility sample (~42% unit overlap and ~76% served-population overlap), sharing slow-moving SDWIS system attributes (private vs. public ownership, groundwater reliance) and partially overlapping 5-year ACS demographic windows (2013–2017 vs. 2011–2015). However, double-counting risk in synthesis is low because the tariff schedules were compiled independently in different cross-sectional years (2019 vs. 2015) and the dependent variables measure distinct constructs: Study A models rate-structure progressivity (the Unit Price Ratio of average unit price at 30,000 vs. 6,000 gallons/month), whereas Study B models annual water bill level ($ at 60,000 gallons/year) and lowest-quintile income share spent on water (%).
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Cross-sectional census of US community water systems serving >= 40,000 residents from US EPA SDWIS (N = 1,189 total: 1,055 local government and 134 investor-owned, serving 183,314,934 residents; analytical N = 1,183 in the 48 contiguous states). Single-family residential water rate schedules were collected independently in January–April 2019 and linked with 2017 ACS 5-year estimates (2013–2017) and 2009–2018 NOAA PDSI drought data. OLS regressions test the association of mean-to-median income inequality and private ownership with rate progressivity (Unit Price Ratio at 12,000–60,000 vs. 6,000 gallons/month).
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Cross-sectional census of the 500 largest US community water systems by service population from US EPA SDWIS across 48 states and DC (N = 500: 321 government-owned, 121 cooperative, and 58 investor-owned, serving ~140 million residents). Residential water rate schedules were compiled independently in January 2015 and linked with 2011–2015 ACS 5-year estimates (plus 2007–2011 ACS for population growth) and 2015 US Drought Monitor county data. OLS regressions test the association of private ownership, state PUC/pro-private regulation (NJ/PA), infrastructure age, and community socioeconomics (Gini, poverty) with typical annual household water bills (at 60,000 gallons/year) and lowest-quintile household income share spent on water.
